Paper explainer · ECCV 2024 · Image restoration

Histoformer: restoring images in bad weather by sorting pixels into histograms

How Sun et al. make transformer attention long-range and cheap by grouping pixels by intensity instead of location, explained with the paper's equations, figures and a PyTorch re-implementation.

Paper: Shangquan Sun, Wenqi Ren, Xinwei Gao, Rui Wang, Xiaochun Cao · arXiv:2407.10172

1. The problem: one model for every kind of bad weather

Rain streaks, raindrops on the lens, fog and snow all degrade images that downstream systems such as detectors and depth estimators depend on. Early work trained a separate network per weather type. The all-in-one setting asks for a single model that restores images affected by any of them, which is the setting Histoformer is built for: one network, trained once on a mixed dataset of snow, rain + fog, and raindrop images.

Transformers are attractive here because weather artefacts are spread across the whole image, so long-range interactions matter. But full spatial self-attention over an H×W image costs O((HW)2), so restoration transformers usually compromise in one of two ways (Fig. 1b):

  • Channel-wise attention (e.g. Restormer's MDTA): attention is computed between channels, which is cheap but mixes spatial information only implicitly.
  • Window attention: attention is computed inside fixed spatial windows, which limits how far apart two related pixels can be.

The paper's key observation is that weather degradation is similar to itself: snowflakes, streaks and drops look alike and are mostly brighter or darker than the background. So instead of grouping pixels by location, Histoformer groups them by intensity, sorting them into histogram bins and applying attention within and across these bins (Fig. 1c). Pixels hit by the same kind of degradation end up in the same bin even if they are far apart in the image.

2. The baseline it builds on

Histoformer keeps the overall skeleton of Restormer (Zamir et al., CVPR 2022), a strong U-shaped restoration transformer, and replaces its two core layers:

Restormer (baseline)Histoformer
Macro layout4-level encoder–decoder, pixel-(un)shuffle resampling, skip connections, global residualSame, plus crude skip-connections from the input image into every encoder stage after the first
AttentionMDTA: attention across channels (a C×C map)DHSA: dynamic-range convolution + histogram self-attention over intensity bins
Feed-forwardGDFN: gated FFN with a 3×3 depth-wise convDGFF: two scales (5×5 and dilated 3×3) on a pixel-shuffled grid, Mish gating
LossL1L1 + Pearson correlation loss
TrainingProgressive patch-size learningProgressive learning, starting at batch 8 / patch 128

The ablations in Section 6 swap each new piece back for the baseline version (MDTA, GDFN, no correlation loss), which isolates the contribution of every component.

3. The proposed components

3.1 Dynamic-range convolution

Before attention, DHSA computes its queries, keys and values with a 1×1 conv followed by a 3×3 depth-wise conv, as in Restormer. Histoformer first sorts half of the channels along the vertical and horizontal axes. After sorting, small values gather in one corner and large values in the opposite corner, so a 3×3 kernel now mixes pixels that are similar in intensity rather than pixels that are merely adjacent. The other half of the channels is left in place, so local structure is still available.

​F1​,F2​=Split(F),F1​=Sortv​(Sorth​(F1​)),F=Conv3×3d​(Conv1×1​(Concat(F1​,F2​)))​

Eq. (3)

Degraded pixels tend to sit next to each other after sorting, so the convolution can treat them separately from clean pixels. The convolution outputs 5C channels: two query–key pairs and one value tensor for the next step. The sort indices are kept so the features can be put back in place at the end of the block.

Dynamic-range convolutionPython · from the notebook
def sort_spatial(x_half, order='hw'):
    '''Sort a (B,C',H,W) tensor along H then W ('hw') or W then H ('wh'). Returns sorted tensor + indices.'''
    if order == 'hw':
        xs, idx_a = x_half.sort(-2)        # along H (each column)
        xs, idx_b = xs.sort(-1)            # along W (each row)
    ...
    return xs, (idx_a, idx_b)

# inside Attention_histogram.forward
        # Eq. 3: dynamic-range convolution
        x1_sorted, idx_sp = sort_spatial(x[:, :c // 2], self.sort_order)
        x = torch.cat([x1_sorted, x[:, c // 2:]], dim=1)
        qkv = self.qkv_dwconv(self.qkv(x))
        q1, k1, q2, k2, v = qkv.chunk(5, dim=1)

3.2 Histogram self-attention (BHR + FHR)

Building the histogram. The value tensor is flattened to C×HW and sorted per channel. The same permutation d is applied to both query–key pairs, so every token stays aligned with its value:

​V,d=Sort(RC×H×WC×HW​(V)),Q1​,K1​=Split(Gather(RC×H×WC×HW​(FQK,1​),d)),Q2​,K2​=Split(Gather(RC×H×WC×HW​(FQK,2​),d))​

Eq. (4)

Two ways to cut it into bins. With B bins the sorted sequence is reshaped to C×B×HW/B, in two complementary ways:

  • Bin-wise histogram reshaping (BHR): B bins, each holding HW/B consecutive pixels in the sorted order. Each bin spans a wide intensity range and many locations, so this branch gathers global context.
  • Frequency-wise histogram reshaping (FHR): HW/B bins of only B pixels each. Each bin holds near-identical intensities, so this branch captures fine-grained detail.
AB​AF​A​=softmax(k​RB​(Q1​)RB​(K1​)⊤​)RB​(V),=softmax(k​RF​(Q2​)RF​(K2​)⊤​)RF​(V),=AB​⊙AF​​

Eq. (5)

Here k is the number of heads. The two branch outputs are scattered back to their original pixel positions, multiplied element-wise, the dynamic-range sort is undone, and a final 1×1 conv projects the result. Because the attention map is computed between (channel, bin) tokens, its size does not grow with HW: the attention cost grows only linearly with the number of pixels, while every token can still draw on pixels from anywhere in the image.

Histogram self-attentionPython · from the notebook
    def reshape_attn(self, q, k, v, ifBox):
        '''Histogram reshaping (BHR if ifBox else FHR) + self-attention, Eq. 5.'''
        ...
        shape_ori = 'b (head c) (factor hw)' if ifBox else 'b (head c) (hw factor)'   # BHR | FHR
        shape_tar = 'b head (c factor) hw'
        q, k, v = (rearrange(t, f'{shape_ori} -> {shape_tar}', factor=self.factor, hw=hw, head=self.num_heads)
                   for t in (q, k, v))
        ...
            attn = torch.softmax((q @ k.transpose(-2, -1)) / math.sqrt(self.num_heads), dim=-1)
        out = attn @ v
        ...

    def forward(self, x):
        ...
        # Eq. 4: sort V per channel, gather Q/K with the same index
        v, idx = v.reshape(b, c, -1).sort(dim=-1)
        q1, k1, q2, k2 = (torch.gather(t.reshape(b, c, -1), 2, idx) for t in (q1, k1, q2, k2))
        # Eq. 5: BHR and FHR branches, scatter back to pixel order, element-wise product
        out1 = self.reshape_attn(q1, k1, v, True)
        out2 = self.reshape_attn(q2, k2, v, False)
        out1 = torch.scatter(out1, 2, idx, out1).view(b, c, h, w)
        out2 = torch.scatter(out2, 2, idx, out2).view(b, c, h, w)
        out = out1 * out2
        ...
            out = torch.cat([unsort_spatial(out[:, :c // 2], idx_sp, self.sort_order), out[:, c // 2:]], 1)
            return self.project_out(out)

In the einops patterns, '(factor hw)' splits the sorted sequence into contiguous chunks (BHR), while '(hw factor)' groups consecutive neighbours together (FHR). Both lead to the same (c factor) × hw layout for the attention product.

3.3 Dual-scale Gated Feed-Forward (DGFF)

The feed-forward network is where a transformer block mixes local context. DGFF expands channels by a factor r with a 1×1 conv, then pixel-shuffles, trading channels for a 2× larger grid so the depth-wise kernels work at a finer scale. The result is split into two branches with different receptive fields: a 5×5 depth-wise conv and a dilated 3×3 depth-wise conv. The Mish-activated dilated branch gates the 5×5 branch, then pixel-unshuffle and a 1×1 conv bring the features back to C channels.

​Fl,1​,Fl,2​=Split(Shuffle(Conv1×1​(Fl​))),Fl,1​=Conv5×5d​(Fl,1​),Fl,2​=Conv3×3d,dilated​(Fl,2​),Fl+1​=Conv1×1​(Unshuffle(Mish(Fl,2​)⊙Fl,1​))​

Eq. (6)

DGFFPython · from the notebook
class FeedForward(nn.Module):
    '''Dual-scale Gated Feed-Forward (DGFF), Eq. 6.'''
    ...
    def forward(self, x):
        x = self.p_shuffle(self.project_in(x))          # Conv1x1 -> Shuffle
        x1, x2 = x.chunk(2, dim=1)                       # Split
        x1 = self.dwconv_5(x1)                           # 5x5 depth-wise
        x2 = self.dwconv_dilated2_1(x2)                  # dilated 3x3 depth-wise
        x = F.mish(x2) * x1                              # gating
        return self.project_out(self.p_unshuffle(x))     # Unshuffle -> Conv1x1

3.4 Histogram Transformer Block (HTB)

DHSA and DGFF are combined in a standard pre-norm residual block:

Fl​=Fl−1​+DHSA(LN(Fl−1​)),Fl​=Fl​+DGFF(LN(Fl​))

Eqs. (1)–(2)

Histogram Transformer BlockPython · from the notebook
class TransformerBlock(nn.Module):
    ...
    def forward(self, x):
        x = x + self.attn_g(self.norm_g(x))       # Eq. 1
        return x + self.ffn(self.norm_ff1(x))     # Eq. 2

3.5 Crude skip-connections

Every encoder stage after the first also receives a cheap view of the input image: average pooling, a 1×1 (pixel-wise) conv and a 3×3 depth-wise conv. The pooling is chained, so stage s sees the image at 1/2s resolution. These features are concatenated with the down-sampled encoder features and fused by a 1×1 conv. Because the original image content is always available, the encoder can concentrate on modelling the weather-induced residual.

Crude skip-connectionPython · from the notebook
class SkipPatchEmbed(nn.Module):
    '''Crude skip-connection: AvgPool -> 1x1 conv -> 3x3 depth-wise conv (§3.1).'''
    def __init__(self, in_c=3, dim=48, bias=False):
        super().__init__()
        self.proj = nn.Sequential(
            nn.AvgPool2d(2, stride=2, padding=0, ceil_mode=False, count_include_pad=True),
            nn.Conv2d(in_c, dim, kernel_size=1, bias=bias),
            nn.Conv2d(dim, dim, kernel_size=3, stride=1, padding=1, groups=dim, bias=bias))

4. Full architecture

A 3×3 conv embeds the low-quality image Ilq∈R3×H×W into C=36 channels. Four encoder levels of {4,4,6,8} HTBs follow, with {1,2,4,8} attention heads and channel widths C,2C,4C,8C. Pixel-unshuffle halves the resolution between levels and pixel-shuffle doubles it again in the decoder. Encoder and decoder levels are joined by skip connections (concatenation + 1×1 conv), the crude skip-connections feed the image into encoder levels 2–4, and refinement blocks precede the 3×3 output conv. The network predicts a residual, so Ihq=Ilq+(network output).

StageLayersFeature size (C = 36)
Patch embedding3×3 convC × H × W
Encoder level 14 HTB, 1 headC × H × W
Encoder level 24 HTB, 2 heads2C × H/2 × W/2
Encoder level 36 HTB, 4 heads4C × H/4 × W/4
Latent (level 4)8 HTB, 8 heads8C × H/8 × W/8
Decoder level 36 HTB, 4 heads4C × H/4 × W/4
Decoder level 24 HTB, 2 heads2C × H/2 × W/2
Decoder level 14 HTB, 1 headC × H × W
Refinement4 HTB, 1 headC × H × W
Output3×3 conv + input image3 × H × W

Feature sizes for a 128×128 input, as printed by the stage-by-stage shape check in the notebook: 36×128×128 → 72×64×64 → 144×32×32 → 288×16×16 and back.

Histoformer.forwardPython · from the notebook
    def forward(self, inp_img):
        e1 = self.encoder_level1(self.patch_embed(inp_img))
        s1 = self.skip_patch_embed1(inp_img)
        e2 = self.encoder_level2(self.reduce_chan_level_1(torch.cat([self.down1_2(e1), s1], 1)))
        s2 = self.skip_patch_embed2(s1)
        e3 = self.encoder_level3(self.reduce_chan_level_2(torch.cat([self.down2_3(e2), s2], 1)))
        s3 = self.skip_patch_embed3(s2)
        lat = self.latent(self.reduce_chan_level_3(torch.cat([self.down3_4(e3), s3], 1)))
        d3 = self.decoder_level3(self.reduce_chan_level3(torch.cat([self.up4_3(lat), e3], 1)))
        d2 = self.decoder_level2(self.reduce_chan_level2(torch.cat([self.up3_2(d3), e2], 1)))
        d1 = torch.cat([self.up2_1(d2), e1], 1)
        if self.cfg.dec1_reduce:
            d1 = self.reduce_chan_level1(d1)
        d1 = self.refinement(self.decoder_level1(d1))
        return self.output(d1) + inp_img

5. Losses and training setup

Reconstruction loss. A standard L1 distance between the restored image Ihq and the ground truth Igt:

Lrec​=​Ihq−Igt​1​

Eq. (7)

Correlation loss. L1 checks each pixel on its own and ignores how pixels relate to each other. Weather degradation disturbs exactly this relationship: a snowflake makes a dark pixel brighter than its neighbours. Histoformer therefore also asks the output to be linearly correlated with the ground truth, so that restored pixels follow the same intensity ordering as the clean image. The Pearson coefficient is computed over all 3HW values of an image:

ρ(Ihq,Igt)=3HWσ(Ihq)σ(Igt)∑i=13HW​(Iihq​−Ihq)(Iigt​−Igt)​

Eq. (8)

Lcor​=21​(1−ρ(Ihq,Igt)),L=Lrec​+αLcor​

Eqs. (9)–(10)

Lcor​ lies in [0,1] and is zero when the output is perfectly correlated with the target. The paper sets α=1; Table 6 shows the result is not sensitive to the exact weight.

Losses (Eqs. 7–10)Python · from the notebook
def reconstruction_loss(pred, gt):                       # Eq. 7
    return (pred - gt).abs().mean()

def pearson_rho(pred, gt, eps=1e-12):                    # Eq. 8, one value per image
    b = pred.shape[0]
    x, y = pred.reshape(b, -1), gt.reshape(b, -1)
    xc, yc = x - x.mean(-1, keepdim=True), y - y.mean(-1, keepdim=True)
    n = x.shape[-1]
    sx = xc.pow(2).mean(-1).sqrt(); sy = yc.pow(2).mean(-1).sqrt()   # population std
    return (xc * yc).sum(-1) / (n * sx * sy + eps)

def correlation_loss(pred, gt, repo_style=False):        # Eq. 9
    ...
    return (0.5 * (1. - pearson_rho(pred, gt))).mean()

def total_loss(pred, gt, cfg=CFG):                       # Eq. 10
    l_rec = reconstruction_loss(pred, gt)
    ...
    return l_rec + cfg.alpha_cor * l_cor, {'l_rec': l_rec.item(), 'l_cor': l_cor.item()}

Hyper-parameters

Training uses the all-weather set: 9,000 Snow100K images, 1,069 RainDrop images and 9,000 Outdoor-Rain (rain + fog) images. Testing uses Snow100K-S/-L, Outdoor-Rain Test1 and the RainDrop test set. PSNR and SSIM are computed on the Y channel.

6. Results reported in the paper

All numbers in this section are the paper's reported results. Histoformer is a single model trained once on all weather types. It is compared with task-specific networks (top half of each table, each trained on one dataset) and with other unified all-weather models (bottom half).

37.41 dBSnow100K-S PSNR
32.16 dBSnow100K-L PSNR
32.08 dBOutdoor-Rain PSNR
33.06 dBRainDrop PSNR

Histoformer's numbers as reported in Table 1 of the paper.

On Snow100K-S, Outdoor-Rain and RainDrop, Histoformer has the best PSNR and SSIM among the unified models. On Snow100K-L it has the best PSNR and the second-best SSIM.

Ablation studies (Outdoor-Rain)

Each ablation replaces one component and reports PSNR/SSIM on Outdoor-Rain, where the full model reaches 32.08 dB / 0.9389:

  • Dynamic-range convolution (Table 2): sorting before the convolution gives +0.14 dB over a vanilla conv. The sorting order makes little difference.
  • Self-attention design (Table 3): DHSA beats MDTA (Restormer) by 1.14 dB and top-k sparse attention (TKSA) by 0.96 dB. Removing either the BHR or the FHR branch hurts, confirming that the two reshapes are complementary.
  • Channels × bins (Table 4): performance rises steadily from 12 to 36; 44 runs out of memory.
  • Feed-forward (Table 5): DGFF beats FFN, GDFN, DANB and MSFN; +0.3 dB over the strongest alternative (MSFN).
  • Correlation loss (Table 6): adding Lcor​ gives +0.31 dB, and every weight between 0.1 and 10 improves on no correlation loss.

7. Takeaways

  • Group by intensity, not by location. Sorting pixels into histogram bins lets attention connect similar degradations anywhere in the image at linear cost.
  • Two views of the histogram. BHR sees coarse, global intensity groups and FHR sees fine, near-identical intensities. Multiplying the two gives better results than either alone.
  • Sorting helps convolutions too. A one-line sort before the depth-wise conv lets the convolution work on similar pixels instead of neighbouring ones.
  • Structure-aware loss. Adding a Pearson correlation term to L1 encourages restored images to keep the ground truth's intensity ordering.

Reference. S. Sun, W. Ren, X. Gao, R. Wang, X. Cao. Restoring Images in Adverse Weather Conditions via Histogram Transformer. ECCV 2024. arXiv:2407.10172. Code: github.com/sunshangquan/Histoformer.
